analysis.one_liner: Lets patients sue HMOs and health plans for damages when cost-cutting causes medically inappropriate denial of care.
analysis.headline: A bill to let patients sue health plans for denying care to cut costs, with 31 cosponsors, was referred to two House committees in May 1997 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1997, managed care plans and HMOs made decisions about what care to approve or deny, and those decisions were often driven by cost. Under the federal benefits law ERISA, patients generally could not recover real damages from a plan for a harmful denial. This bill would have changed that: it would let patients sue the plan or its insurer for actual damages, and in some cases punitive damages, when care is denied because of a medically inappropriate cost-containment decision. It would also require plans to fully indemnify doctors for liability caused by plan rules that restrict what doctors can tell patients, and it would add an excise tax on cost-driven violations of plan terms.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in managed care plans and HMOs, and their families. If care is denied or cut back because of a cost-driven decision that a doctor would consider medically inappropriate, the patient could sue in state or federal court and recover actual damages, and in some cases punitive damages. Doctors also benefit: they would be protected from personal liability when a plan's rules restrict what they can tell patients, so they could speak freely about treatment options and the plan's financial incentives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in HMOs and managed care plans

how_it_helps.text: Lets patients recover actual damages (including compensatory and consequential damages) from a plan or its insurer when a benefit is denied because of a medically inappropriate cost-containment decision, with punitive damages allowed at the court's discretion.
Makes the plan and the insurance issuer jointly and severally liable, so patients can collect from whichever defendant contributed to the denial instead of being passed between them.

Requires plans to fully indemnify doctors for liability caused by plan gag rules on medical communications, removing financial pressure on physicians to stay quiet about treatment options, risks, benefits, and the plan's financial incentives.
Imposes an excise tax under the Internal Revenue Code on insurers and plans that fail to provide benefits because of improper cost-driven delivery decisions, adding a penalty layer beyond lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and self-insured employers would bear the cost: they would face joint and several liability for compensatory and possibly punitive damages when cost-driven decisions deny medically appropriate care, plus a new excise tax for such violations. Higher liability costs would likely flow into higher premiums for employers and workers.

drawbacks.text: Joint and several liability, consequential damages, and possible punitive damages for cost-driven denials could push health plan costs up significantly, which would flow into higher premiums for employers and workers.

Because the liability standard turns on whether a decision was 'clinically or medically inappropriate,' after-the-fact litigation over medical judgment could encourage defensive medicine and add administrative costs.

Self-insured employers, as plan sponsors, would face new liability exposure for managed care decisions they currently escape under ERISA, which could lead some employers to reduce or drop health benefits rather than bear the risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real accountability: in the late 1990s, HMO cost-containment decisions were effectively shielded from damages under ERISA, and the bill would have given patients a way to recover when a cost-driven denial caused harm, while also protecting doctors who wanted to speak honestly about treatment options. The cost is that liability exposure, especially joint and several liability plus possible punitive damages and an excise tax, would likely have raised premiums and could have pushed some employers to drop coverage or shrink benefits rather than face lawsuit risk, and the retrospective "was it medically appropriate" standard would have invited litigation after the fact. A well-designed version could have paired accountability with safeguards against frivolous suits; as introduced, the bill did not include them, and an honest supporter would acknowledge the premium and litigation costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means committees, sent to the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee in June 1997, and then sat with no further action until that Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 22, 1997 with Pete Stark and a group of Democratic members as original cosponsors.
On May 22, 1997 it was referred to two committees, Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means, meaning both would have to act before the bill could move.

On June 17, 1997 the Education and the Workforce portion was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, and the action history shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and HMOs came out ahead: they kept the shield against damages for cost-driven denial decisions and never paid the excise tax. Patients who received medically inappropriate denials of care were left without the new legal remedy the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), senior member of the Ways and Means health subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 22, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors such as Pelosi, Waxman, Rangel, Frank, Kucinich, and Sanders.

against.name: Bill Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on May 22, 1997 and referred it to the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on May 22, 1997 for the tax-related provisions and the record shows no action on it thereafter.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Insurers, HMOs, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed expansion of legal liability for managed care decisions during the 1990s patients'-rights debate, arguing it would raise costs and fuel lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats, no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committees run by Republican chairs.

industries.note: The bill strips away the practical shield managed care plans had against damages for cost-driven denial decisions, exposing insurers to compensatory, consequential, and possible punitive damages plus an excise tax. Patients would gain a real remedy when a cost-driven denial caused harm.

industries.industry: Employers that sponsor self-insured health plans
industries.note: As 'plan sponsors' they would be 'specified defendants' facing joint and several liability for cost-driven failures to provide benefits, a risk they do not bear under current ERISA law. Some could respond by cutting or dropping coverage.

The bill requires plans to fully indemnify providers for liability caused by plan restrictions on medical communications, freeing doctors to discuss treatment options, plan decisions, and financial incentives without personal financial risk.
